text.p: The Vermont Legislature has been offered a securitization proposal that could reduce electricity costs in Vermont next year by $25 million or more, Green Mountain Power Corp Chief Executive Douglas Hyde told the utility's annual meeting.

The company, joined by Central Vermont Public Service Corp, put forward the plan as a way to lower rates after the Legislature had shelved a more sweeping proposal that would restructure the electric industry in Vermont, Hyde explained at last week's meeting.

"After the House leadership concluded it could not pass a full restructuring bill this year, we proposed an alternative approach that might have eliminated the need for an immediate rate increase. It would have put in place a financing mechanism that has been enacted in other states and which offered the prospect of reducing the escalation in power supply costs."
The utilities are calling the mechanism a grantor trust, Green Mountain Chief Financial Office Chris Dutton told Reuters Monday, explaining it is a form of securitization.
Hyde said the Legislative leadership so far has not taken the rate-reduction plan to the full membership.

He told shareholders passage of the plan would not guarantee lower rates, but failure to pass the proposal would eliminate use of this innovative financing mechanism and leave Green Mountain no option other than filing immediately for a rate increase.

"If the Legislature goes home, and I know the hour is late, without enacting this proposal, we will be foreclosed from using this financing mechanism to reduce costs in 1998," he said. ((-- Jim Brumm 212-859-1710.))
